The payment for the Ooty trip was due the next morning, and the rain had flooded the lane outside school. Harish stood under the tin shed, soaked, knowing his mother couldn't pay it this month. Not since the mill closed.
Anjali splashed over. "Harish, I heard. My parents said they'd happily pay your share. Really."
His face burned. Kind, yes. But everyone would know.
"Thanks," he said stiffly. "I'll manage."
Anjali's face fell. They stood watching the rain in silence.
Then Harish thought about how he'd feel if it were the other way round. He'd want to help too.
"Anjali, sorry. That came out wrong. I can't take the trip money. It's too much. But could I borrow your chemistry guide for the exam? We can't buy it this term."
"Of course," she said at once.
"And please don't look at me like I'm a sad story. I'm still me."
She laughed. "You're still annoying, you mean."

qa.q: What did Anjali's parents offer to pay for?
qa.a: Harish's share of the Ooty trip.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Anjali offered to help?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and his pride stung, afraid everyone would know about his family's troubles.

qa.q: What balance did Harish find, and why is it wise?
qa.a: He accepted the chemistry guide, which felt fair, turned down the bigger gift, and asked not to be pitied, without rejecting her kindness.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Harish first refuses?
qa.a: Anjali seems hurt and awkward, since she only wanted to help and his stiff answer shut her out.

grounding: A teen whose family is struggling feels his pride stung by a friend's offer, accepts fair help and asks not to be pitied.

Since Yash's mother went into hospital, Eshaan had brought him a tiffin every day. Aloo paratha, curd rice, sometimes sweets. At first Yash was grateful. His father was working double shifts and nobody at home had time to cook.
But lately Eshaan kept saying things like, "Poor you, yaar," and, in front of others, "Yash can't come, his mother's sick, na?" People looked at Yash with that soft, sad face. He hated it.
On Thursday, when Eshaan handed him the tiffin in the Bengaluru school canteen, Yash felt his throat tighten.
"Thank you. Honestly. This food is saving me," he said. "But can I ask one thing? Please don't tell people about Amma or say 'poor you.' I just want to be normal."
Eshaan blinked. "Oh. Sorry. I didn't think."
"It's okay." Yash opened the tiffin. "Is this your mum's pulao? Tell her it's the best in Bengaluru."

qa.a: A tiffin.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Eshaan said 'Poor you' in front of others?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, hating the pitying looks even though he was grateful for the food.

qa.q: What did Yash do that balanced gratitude and pride?
qa.a: He thanked Eshaan sincerely and kept accepting the food, but asked him clearly not to talk about Amma or pity him.

qa.q: How does Eshaan react to Yash's request?
qa.a: Eshaan is surprised and apologetic, having not realised his words made Yash feel pitied.

Uma found her in the corridor ten minutes before the results. "You'll win, obviously. You always win everything, na?" She smiled, but her eyes didn't.
Nikita felt the little sting in it. Lately there were a lot of compliments like that, sweet on top, sour underneath.

She walked over to Uma. "You gave the best speech today," she said honestly. "Your point about the library was better than mine."

Sports day, and the whole junior school was watching Ishita. She was the Class 11 sprint champion, and the Class 6 kids followed her everywhere, copying her ponytail, chanting her name. Baljeet from 6B even carried her water bottle.
She loved it. She also noticed how much she started to need it: checking if they were watching before she ran, feeling flat on days they weren't.
Then, in the final 100 metres, she stumbled at the start and came fourth.
The juniors went silent. Ishita wanted to disappear, to pretend she'd pulled a muscle, anything to keep the picture perfect.
Instead, she walked over to them, breathless. "Well, that happened," she said. "I messed up my start. I do that sometimes. I'm still learning too, you know."
Baljeet looked surprised, then grinned. "You still run faster than my brother."
Ishita laughed properly. Losing in front of them felt oddly freeing.

qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling about the juniors' attention before the race?
qa.a: She loved it but felt uneasy, noticing she had started to need their audience to feel good.

qa.a: She admitted her mistake to the juniors instead of hiding it, showing humility and that she is still learning too.

For two months, Arnab ate lunch alone on the steps behind the Kolkata school's science block. Nobody was cruel. Nobody noticed him either. The ache of it sat in his chest all afternoon.
Some days he thought, maybe I'm just not someone people like.
One Wednesday he saw a notice on the board: Chess Club, Room 12, lunch. He stood in front of it for a long time. Then he went.
There were only four people. A tall boy named Hemant was setting up a board alone. Arnab took a breath. "Want to play?"
Hemant shrugged. "Sure. Warning, I'm bad."
He wasn't bad. Arnab lost twice. They argued about the Sicilian opening until the bell.
That evening, Arnab told his class teacher about the months on the steps. She listened and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'll keep an eye out, and let's talk again next week."
The next day, he went back to Room 12.

qa.a: On the steps behind the Kolkata school's science block.

Dear Pintu,
I owe you an apology, so here it is on paper.
Since September, I've been following Nikita didi from Class 12 around like a shadow. She's head of the football team, everyone listens to her, and I wanted to be just like her. I started talking like her, walking like her, even cut my hair like hers.
And I stopped hanging out with you. When you asked me to come to the science fair, I said I was busy. I was actually waiting outside the football field hoping she'd notice me.
Last week I heard her mocking the Class 8 kids, and I laughed along. Then I felt sick. I don't want to be the kind of person who laughs at kids for her attention.
I still admire how she leads the team. I'll keep that. But the rest I'm dropping.
Science fair's in two weeks. Can I still help with your volcano?
Santosh
